🇯🇵 | In Japan, some companies mark the retirement of long-serving machinery with small farewell ceremonies. 

In one recent viral example, employees gathered as a 92-year-old former factory manager performed a traditional purification ritual known as “kiyoharai” before two old machines were finally removed after decades of service.

The gesture reflects a wider Japanese tradition of expressing gratitude toward objects and tools that have played an important role in people’s lives. Similar memorial ceremonies, often linked to the practice of “kuyō”, have historically been held for items such as sewing needles, dolls, clocks and even industrial equipment.

Rather than suggesting that these objects are literally alive, the tradition is about respecting their years of service and acknowledging the memories, work and people connected to them before they are discarded, recycled or replaced.
